name: Azurite Blue
lede: Azurite is a bright blue copper carbonate mineral that painters ground into one of Europe's main blues before ultramarine and Prussian blue; the color name now points at a darker, duller swatch than the stone.

sections.title: The mineral
sections.body:
Azurite is a hydrated copper carbonate, Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2, the blue twin of the green mineral malachite [1]. Its synthetic counterpart was widely used as a pigment under the name blue verditer [1]. Synonyms from older sources include mountain blue, blue ashes, Italian blue and Bremen blue [2][3].

Egyptians had already ground azurite and malachite among their natural pigments [4].

sections.title: Rival to lapis
sections.body: In Renaissance Florence the Jesuati of the convent of San Giusto alle Mura made a speciality of the best lapis lazuli and azurite blues, as Gage describes in his history of artists' suppliers [5]. From the seventeenth century, Balfour-Paul reports, the prices of ultramarine and azurite blues were often so high that artists turned to the cheaper indigo [6].

sections.title: The swatch is darker than the stone
sections.body: The library entry combines Ridgway's 1912 plate IX, ISCC-NBS block 173 and the Maerz and Paul dictionary, which dates the name to 1816 [7]. All three show a dark, greyed blue, much duller than the bright mineral the Compendium describes [1][7]. Its nearest everyday name is [[dusk]], and [[cobalt]] is ten units away [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this swatch, covering five per cent of the canvas or more, in 67 of 23,781 paintings [8]. Henri Matisse carries it in 5 of his 50 paintings, about 35 times the average rate [8]. The decade of the 1910s peaks, in 11 of 523 paintings [8]. These are photographed paintings, not pigment tests, and a dark blue match says nothing about whether azurite was used [8].
